gt_events.gt_event: ± 17:20 UTC: an engineer takes an LVM snapshot of the production database and loads it into staging - later the only recoverable copy (~6 hours old at wipe time)
± 19:00 UTC: GitLab.com starts experiencing an increase in database load due to suspected spam, plus a background job removing a GitLab employee flagged for abuse; users unable to post comments

± 23:00 UTC: the PostgreSQL secondary's replication fails (WAL segments already removed on the primary, no WAL archiving); manual resync via pg_basebackup hangs; max_wal_senders raised 3 -> 32, max_connections lowered 8000 -> 2000

± 23:30 UTC: trying to restore replication, an engineer wipes the PostgreSQL data directory on the PRIMARY by accident instead of the secondary; the process is terminated a second or two later but around 300 GB of data is removed

Backup hunt fails: the pg_dump S3 bucket is empty (pg_dump 9.2 vs PostgreSQL 9.6 version mismatch; failure emails rejected for missing DMARC signing), Azure disk snapshots are not enabled for the database servers, and the secondary is wiped
Recovery starts from the 6-hour-old LVM snapshot via the staging host on slow Azure classic disks (~60 Mbps); copying the data directory to production takes around 18 hours
17:00 UTC: the GitLab.com database is restored (without webhooks) to its state of January 31st 17:20 UTC
Around 18:00 UTC: webhooks restored from a separate staging database built from the same snapshot; final checks complete and the service is re-enabled
The postmortem is published on the GitLab blog (original permalink referenced by the tracking issue)
